title: SRE documentation standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, runbooks and tooling
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary
This page defines Redwood Inference's SRE documentation standards: how we write and maintain SLOs and error budgets, conduct capacity planning, run reliability initiatives, perform incident reviews, and author operational runbooks and tooling references. The goal is consistent, actionable, and audit-ready SRE documentation that supports predictable reliability and safe product velocity.

Scope and audience
- Scope: All customer-facing inference services, control-plane APIs, and platform observability/ingestion pipelines owned or operated by Redwood.
- Audience: SREs, service owners, product managers, on-call engineers, and Eng leadership.

Principles
1) Single source of truth: Every service must have a canonical confluence runbook + linked dashboards and a traceable SLO definition.
2) Measurable and testable SLIs: SLIs must be instrumented as metrics and synthetic checks and included in dashboards.
3) Blameless, timely reviews: Post-incident reviews are blameless, owned, and completed within timeboxes.
4) Actionable runbooks: Runbooks must include deterministic mitigation steps and clear escalation paths.
5) Continuous improvement: Reliability initiatives are prioritized from postmortems and SLO burn analysis.

1. SLOs and Error Budgets
1.1 SLI & SLO definitions (required fields)
For each SLO document the following fields explicitly:
- Service name (human-friendly)
- SLI (definition, numerator, denominator) include instrumentation location (metric name / telemetry tag)
- SLO target (percentage) and measurement window (rolling 30d or calendar month)
- Owner (team, primary and secondary)
- Exclusions (maintenance windows, allowed test traffic, known downstream outages)
- Alerting and reporting (error-budget burn alerts, dashboard links)

Example SLO table (text table to be copied into service pages)
| Service | SLI | SLO | Window | Owner | Notes |
| Inference API (text-gen) | Successful responses (status 2xx & non-empty body) / total requests | 99.95% | 30d rolling | eng-serving-runtime | Exclude canary tests by header X-Canary:true |
| Inference API (latency p99) | p99 latency < 300ms | 99.0% | 30d rolling | eng-serving-runtime | Measure at edge egress |

1.2 Measurement and instrumentation
- All SLIs must be collected in Prometheus/OTel metrics and synthetic checks in Grafana Synthetic or equivalent. Include the metric path, labels used for aggregation, and the query used for the SLO.
- Document precisely which requests are in-scope (e.g., customer vs internal, production vs staging). Provide example PromQL/SQL used for calculations.

1.3 Error budget policy (standardized actions)
Error budgets are the operational mechanism to balance velocity and reliability. The default monthly policy:
- Green (burn rate <= 1): normal deploy cadence
- Watch (burn rate > 1 and <= 2 for 6h): increased monitoring, product and SRE notified, hold large experiments for 24h
- Restrict (burn rate > 2 for 6h OR cumulative burn >= 50% of monthly budget): freeze non-critical deployments; require SRE approval for any change that touches the SLO boundary
- Emergency (rapid burn leading to SLO breach within 24h): immediate mitigations per runbook, executive notification, and mandatory incident review after recovery

Escalation actions (who to call)
1) PagerDuty primary for service -> immediate follow the runbook
2) SRE lead on-call (pager) -> coordinate cross-service mitigation
3) Product manager -> evaluate feature rollbacks or mitigations
4) Eng leadership -> decide extended restrictions or customer communications

1.4 SLO review cadence
- Each service SLO must be reviewed quarterly by service owner + SRE. Change requests must include reason, data demonstrating the need, and an updated roll-out plan.

2. Capacity planning
2.1 Objectives and inputs
Capacity planning ensures we meet SLOs under expected and peak load while optimizing cost. Inputs: historical QPS/time-of-day, p50/p95/p99 latency distributions, model sequence length distributions, KV cache hit ratios, expected product growth, and scheduled events (marketing campaigns, customer rollouts).

2.2 Basic capacity model (statistical safety factor)
- Define baseline_qps = p95 QPS over the busiest hour
- Required_capacity = baseline_qps * (1 + expected_growth) * safety_factor
- safety_factor: default 1.5 for hostable services; 2.0 for latency-sensitive inference endpoints during model rollout windows

2.3 GPU pool sizing (example)
- Estimate per-request GPU utilization: tokens_per_request * average_compute_cost_per_token (ms/token) -> ms/request
- GPU_throughput = 1000 / ms_per_batch (requests/sec per GPU) * average_batch_size
- GPUs_needed = ceil(Required_QPS / GPU_throughput) + buffer (10-20% for headroom)
- Document assumptions (sequence length percentiles, batching strategy, quantization profile) in the capacity plan appendix.

2.4 Planning artifacts and ownership
- Required artifacts: current utilization dashboard link, growth assumptions, cost estimate, risk assessment, autoscaling policy config, and runbook changes if capacity scaling affects on-call processes.
- Owners: service owner prepares plan; SRE reviews and approves. Capacity changes affecting Dedicated or Private customers must be coordinated with Solutions/Account teams.

2.5 Load testing and validation
- Before large capacity changes or model rollouts run synthetic load tests that match p95 token lengths and include cold-cache scenarios. Publish results in the planning doc and link JMeter/Locust scripts.

3. Operational tooling and dashboards
Required tooling & standard dashboards:
- Metrics: Prometheus + Grafana (per-service SLO dashboard, error-budget burn dashboard, capacity utilization)
- Traces: Jaeger/Honeycomb traces with standardized span naming (service.operation)
- Logs: Centralized logs with structured JSON fields (service, request_id, model, sequence_length, customer_id_hash)
- Incident management: PagerDuty for on-call, runbook links in the PD escalation policy
- Synthetic checks: Grafana or third-party synthetic probes for availability and latency from multiple regions
- CI/CD hooks: Automated pre-deploy SLO checks for canary analysis (see canary checklist below)

Standard dashboards to include on each service landing page:
- SLO summary (availability, latency, error budget remaining)
- Traffic breakdown (by region, model, API key tier)
- Capacity & GPU utilization (current, 24h, 7d)
- Recent high-latency traces & common error types

Alerting guidance (example thresholds)
- Availability SLO alert: error-budget burn rate > 2 for 1h -> P2 alert to SRE on-call
- Latency SLO alert: p99 > SLO target for 30m -> P2
- Capacity alert: GPU utilization > 85% sustained for 15m -> autoscaling path or P2 if scaling failed
- Queue/backpressure: request queue length > threshold for 5m -> P1 if impacting SLOs

4. Runbooks (standards & template)
4.1 Runbook standard structure (required sections)
- Title 
- Service and owners (primary, secondary, PagerDuty escalation)
- Runbook version and last_updated date
- Symptoms (how violations are observed: alerts, dashboards, customer reports)
- Impact assessment (who is impacted, estimated scope)
- Immediate mitigations (ordered steps with commands/links)
- Diagnostic commands & queries (promql, trace search, sample logs)
- Escalation matrix (roles, contact info, when to escalate)
- Recovery verification checklist (what to check post-mitigation)
- Post-incident actions and links to postmortem template

4.2 Runbook content guidance
- Each mitigation step must be prescriptive (e.g., toggle config flag, scale pool to N GPUs via infra CLI, rollback canary) and include exact commands and expected outcomes.
- Where possible, include idempotent commands and safety checks.
- Provide quick links to dashboards, playbooks, and related runbooks for dependent services.

4.3 Runbook example excerpt (text)
Title: Inference API high p99 latency
Owners: eng-serving-runtime (primary: pageduty: inference-api-oncall, secondary: eng-sre-lead)
Symptoms: p99 latency above 450ms for > 10m, increased tail errors 5xx
Immediate mitigations:
1. Check error-budget dashboard and recent deploys (link)
2. If recent deploy within last 30m, rollback to previous model binary: infra rollback --service inference-api --version vX
3. Increase GPU pool (hot scale): infra scale --pool inference-gpu --count +2 (wait for ready signal)
4. If queue backlog high, temporarily enable degraded-mode-response: curl -XPOST https://admin/api/feature-flags -d '{"degraded_mode":true}'
Diagnostic queries:
- PromQL: rate(http_requests_total{job=\"inference-api\",status!~\"2..\"}[5m])
- Trace search: service:inference-api AND span.op:decode_model AND duration>200ms

5. Incident review standards and postmortems
5.1 Timing and ownership
- Severity definitions: see table below.
- Incidents classified S1 (customer-impacting, significant loss of revenue or SLA breach), S2 (partial degradation), S3 (minor).
- Postmortem for S1/S2 incidents: draft within 48 hours, final postmortem completed within 7 days. Responsible: incident commander (IC) + SRE.

5.2 Postmortem template (fields)
- Title, incident ID, severity, start/end times, summary (2-3 sentences)
- Timeline / timeline highlights (bullet time-ordered events)
- Root cause analysis (RCA) with evidence (logs, traces, metrics)
- Contributing factors and detection gaps
- Immediate mitigations and long-term fixes (owner + ETA)
- SLO impact (quantify lost availability / tokens)
- Lessons learned and follow-up actions
- Verification plan and closure criteria

5.3 Incident review process and blameless culture
- Facilitate a blameless review workshop within 72 hours for S1 incidents. Include representatives from SRE, product, infra, and affected teams.
- Use RCA techniques (5 whys, timeline correlation, evidence triage).
- Track action items in a central board and require at least one follow-up verification test per action.

6. Reliability initiatives and prioritization
6.1 Sources of reliability work
- Postmortem action items (high priority)
- SLO burn trends and recurring alerts
- Capacity shortfalls identified in planning exercises
- Customer escalations and contractual requirements (Dedicated/Private customers)

6.2 Initiative lifecycle
1) Intake: Document initiative in reliability backlog, include hypothesis and measurable success criteria 
2) Design: Runbook & test plans; pre-deploy capacity/chaos tests if relevant
3) Implementation: owner + SRE pairing, small incremental deploys with canary SLO checks 
4) Verification: measure SLO and error budget improvements for 30d post-change
5) Close: include in quarterly reliability report and knowledge base

6.3 Prioritization framework
- Use a simple scoring: Impact * Probability * Visibility / Effort. Prioritize items that reduce SLO burn and improve customer-facing observability.

7. Canary & rollout guidance (SRE checklist)
- Run canary for minimum 24-72 hours depending on risk; monitor SLOs and error budget burn continuously.
- Automated canary analysis: require canary to pass synthetic tests and 0 unexplained increase in error-rate for 30m before promoting.
- If canary causes sustained SLO degradation, automatically rollback and open an incident.

8. Documentation lifecycle and ownership
- Every service doc (SLO, runbook, capacity plan) must have an explicit owner and review cadence (quarterly for SLOs, after any major infra/model change for runbooks).
- When editing: update last_updated and include a short changelog entry at top of the doc.

Appendices
A. Severity table (short)
- S1: Significant customer impact or SLO breach; immediate exec notification; postmortem required
- S2: Partial degradation affecting subset of customers; IC and SRE response; postmortem required if >4h
- S3: Degraded behavior with limited/no customer impact; documented and tracked

B. Quick links (examples)
- SLO dashboard template: https://grafana.redwood/slo-template
- Runbook template: https://confluence.redwood/templates/sre-runbook
- Incident postmortem template: https://confluence.redwood/templates/postmortem
